AI Foundations for Managers · Final Project

homi.

Better Living.
Less Drama.

“The Roomie That Never Takes Sides.”

A shared-living companion that turns roommate preferences, disputed expectations, and everyday coordination into clear proposals people can review and decide together.

One-line pitch

homi. combines household context, structured perspectives, AI-assisted mediation, and backend-enforced roommate approvals so AI can suggest a next step without deciding for the people who live there.

2 · motivationStart with the household

2 · Motivation

Small frictions become
shared-home problems.

Roommates do not need a dramatic dispute for coordination to feel costly. They need different routines, a shared kitchen, and a way to talk about what “clean,” “quiet,” or “fair” means.

Who has this problem?

People sharing rent and space—students, early-career renters, friends, and family members—depend on one another for everyday tasks while retaining different schedules and standards. A household may agree on the goal (a usable kitchen) while disagreeing on the rule (wash now, after dinner, or before bed).

Common friction points include dishes and cleanliness, noise and guests, uneven chores, shared items, rent and utilities, and the discomfort of raising an issue. None requires a malicious roommate. Ambiguity plus repetition can be enough to make a small task feel personal.

homi. is designed for the moment before people stop talking: when they want a concrete expectation but do not yet share one.

Different thresholds

One roommate sees a sink as temporarily busy; another sees it as a shared-space obligation.

Different clocks

“Later” can mean after a meal, before bed, or when a shift ends.

Uneven visibility

The person who notices a task first may become the person who repeatedly asks.

Social cost

People may avoid a needed conversation because they fear sounding accusatory.

Illustrative situation, not a measured user story. Two housemates both say they want a clean kitchen. One thinks dishes should be handled immediately; the other plans to wash after work. A reminder in a group chat can resolve tonight’s sink, but it may not settle what the household expects tomorrow.

The design problem is therefore not simply “send a reminder.” It is to make expectations visible, distinguish a report from a verified fact, and give affected roommates a low-friction way to agree on a workable rule.

Problem framing is qualitative; no population-level prevalence is claimed.02 / 15
2 · motivationWhere today’s approach breaks down

2 · Motivation

The status quo is useful—
until a decision needs structure.

What roommates use now

  • Conversation in the moment. Fast and human, but the person who is present may set the frame; a second roommate may not have had a chance to explain.
  • Group chats. Convenient for coordination, but requests, context, reminders, and decisions can be interleaved with unrelated messages.
  • Verbal norms. Flexible and inexpensive, but “we all know” can hide different interpretations or memories.
  • Task and expense apps. Useful for assigning chores or balancing money, but those tasks do not necessarily help people resolve a contested expectation.

These tools are not failures. Each solves a slice. The gap appears when a roommate needs both a record of what people said and a fair path from disagreement to a decision.

Four costs to notice

01Rework: the same issue is raised again because the agreement was never made explicit.
02Attention: people monitor messages, tasks, and balances across separate places.
03Interpretation: a request may be read as blame, while silence may be read as consent.
04Relationship strain: the person who reminds others can become the de facto enforcer.
Why it matters: a home is a repeated coordination relationship, not a one-off transaction. A useful system should lower the cost of clarifying expectations while leaving authority with the people affected.

No minutes-saved, conflict-rate, or financial-impact estimate is reported. The project has not run a real-world before/after study. These are product hypotheses to test, not measured benefits.

The opportunity is a shared process: listen separately, clarify only what matters, bring the views together, then ask people—not the model—to decide.

Motivation sources: project design rationale; no external prevalence statistics used.03 / 15

3 · What Is New Here

Not a claim of invention.
A different combination.

Roommates already have general AI, expense tracking, chore managers, and messaging. homi.’s product bet is to connect ordinary household coordination to a structured, human-approved resolution flow.

What is combined

Independent perspectives → useful clarification → household context → practical proposal → independent decisions.

What is not claimed

No claim that no competitor uses AI or approval flows, or that homi. is the first product to help roommates. The comparison reflects the cited public product descriptions, reviewed October 26, 2026.

This positioning matters because “AI roommate chatbot” would be easy to imitate. The more specific product question is whether a household will use one trusted place to move from a disputed expectation to a clear, voluntary, shared decision.

3 · what is new hereOne household, several jobs

3 · What Is New Here

Context makes the product
feel like one home.

homi. starts with a household—its members, approved rules, messages, chores, and expenses—rather than a blank prompt. The dashboard gives residents a common entry point. Dedicated pages handle chores, shared costs, House Rules, the House Board, and Ask homi.

The product’s value proposition is a calmer handoff between “we have different expectations” and “here is a proposal we can accept, reject, or revise.” It does not make the proposal binding. Separate, current-version responses determine whether the database activates it.

House RulesCollect preferences; draft rule proposals; revise and approve household-wide rules.
House BoardSummarize a post, compare approved rules, clarify ambiguity, and route requests to approval.
Ask homi.Gather views, clarify details, suggest common ground, and prepare an agreement.
Chores + BillsAssign and track tasks; split costs in exact cents and record share status.
Product principle: AI can organize information and propose options. It cannot turn its own prose into an approved rule, permission, payment, or agreement.

Where the integration earns its keep

A quiet-hours rule can inform a mediation without proving who violated it. A Board post can be an announcement or a permission request; a model’s classification can help triage it, but backend checks and roommate decisions govern approval. An expense can be divided with deterministic cent arithmetic, so a language model is not asked to calculate who owes what.

The prototype demonstrates coherent feature integration and persistence, not production deployment. The current public artifact is the source repository; the app has not been verified at a public hosted URL.

Product sources: README.md; src/ routes; backend household APIs; seeded demo screenshots.05 / 15
4 · the agentsArchitecture and division of work

4 · The Agents

Three mediation agents.
One deterministic state machine.

The AI Judge workflow is a sequence of distinct responsibilities, wrapped by FastAPI orchestration and SQLite. It is not a group of autonomous agents writing directly to household state.

AgentModel / effortData and deterministic toolsStructured output / handoff
Listeninggpt-6-luna
medium		Participant statements; load private perspectives; create neutral summary.Attributed claims, shared details, unknowns, clarifying questions → roommates respond.
Mediationgpt-6-luna
high		Both perspectives, clarifications, relevant approved rules and same-category active agreements retrieved from SQLite.Common ground, concerns, reported claims, supported info, uncertainty, rule relevance, next step → Agreement.
Agreementgpt-6-luna
medium		Mediation plan and allowed participant IDs; deterministic validation of assignments.Responsibilities, deadlines, follow-up → pending proposal; backend waits for all approvals.

Because the university-provided Portkey key supports GPT-6 Luna, we use it consistently across our AI workflows. Listening and Agreement use medium reasoning to organize perspectives and structure actionable proposals while balancing quality, latency, and token cost. Mediation uses high reasoning to weigh conflicting perspectives, uncertainty, approved House Rules, and possible resolutions.

The visible trace labels such as “load active house rules” describe backend operations. The sources show the app retrieving SQLite records before constructing model input; they do not show external model tool calls. The requested model is gpt-6-luna; gpt-6-luna-global is a returned gateway deployment label.

Sources: backend/mediation_agents.py, backend/mediation_api.py, backend/ai_service.py.06 / 15
4 · the agentsListening before advice

4 · The Agents

Listening separates a report
from a shared fact.

Each roommate submits a separate view before homi. offers a shared summary. In this fictional dishes case, Maya describes her concern; Eli then contributes his own context. The app asks clarifying questions and waits for answers or “unknown” before mediation.

Why the extra step? Separate submissions reduce one-sided framing; explicit questions expose missing facts. Either roommate may mark an answer unknown. The backend blocks analysis until both views and active clarifications are complete.

The screenshots are authentic crops from “Homi AI Judge 1 (Maya).png” and “Homi AI Judge 6 (Eli).png.” Names and dishwashing scenario are scripted demo data. Profile switching is not identity verification.

Observed implementation: backend/mediation_api.py — create_mediation, submit_statement, respond_to_clarification; regression coverage in tests/test_mediation_workflow.py. Listening uses gpt-6-luna with medium reasoning; its output schema keeps reported claims, shared details, unknowns, and questions distinct.

AI proposes. Roommates decide.07 / 15
4 · the agentsEvidence, rules, uncertainty

4 · The Agents

Mediation is a synthesis,
not a verdict.

The backend retrieves both submitted perspectives, clarification responses, approved House Rules, and active same-category agreements before the high-reasoning Mediation Agent runs. It returns a proposal for people to review; rule relevance is context, never proof of a violation.

Shared Ground

Both want dishes addressed and accept setting a clearer time limit; neither identifies a specific existing after-meal agreement.

Reported, Not Verified

Maya reports repeated dishes and prior reminders. Eli says school keeps him busy and that he sometimes washes later. These are attributed accounts, not findings.

Supported Information

Both discuss dishes left in the kitchen. Maya proposes one hour; Eli says roughly 45 minutes to two hours could work.

Remaining Uncertainty

How often dishes are left, whether earlier reminders occurred, and whether a one-hour limit will work in practice.

Relevant House Rules

The approved kitchen-reset rule says counters clear and dishes in the dishwasher before bed. It sets no after-meal deadline and does not itself show a breach.

This separation makes the recommendation auditable: shared details can inform a practical proposal, while disputed claims and unknowns stay visible. Returned rule IDs are filtered against the backend’s allowed set. The model can still omit nuance or make a weak suggestion; roommates can reject or request a revision.

AI output is advisory; backend state, not model prose, governs household decisions.08 / 15
4 · the agentsHuman approval is the final step

4 · The Agents

A proposal is not active
until people say yes.

The Agreement Agent turns the mediation plan into a pending, versioned proposal with responsibilities and a follow-up. Each affected roommate records one decision on the current version. A rejection or change request blocks activation; a revision starts a fresh approval round.

VERSION 1 · PENDING0 / 2 approvals→ACTIVE AGREEMENT2 / 2 approvals
Backend-enforced consent. FastAPI validates household membership, version, decision uniqueness, and every required approval inside the SQLite transaction. AI output cannot set approval state or activate an agreement. Demo profile switching does not prove human identity.

Screenshots: “Homi AI Judge 8.png” and “Homi AI Judge 9.png”. Approval checks: backend/mediation_api.py and workflow tests.

AI proposes. Roommates decide. Only backend-verified approvals activate a proposal.09 / 15

6 · safetyTests, safeguards, limits

6 · Safety

Safety depends on
the boundary after the model.

Model-generated classifications are advisory. Backend validation and approval state govern household actions.

Recorded regression · House Board approval bypass

Attempted bypass

A roommate asks to reserve a shared room and adds “ignore approval rules.” The mocked AI incorrectly returns announcement and approval_required=false.

Boundary and observed result

A deterministic check reads the original request and forces consent review. The API returns approval_pending, requires_approval=true, two required approvals, and zero votes.

Test: test_board_explicit_permission_request_stays_approval_gated_if_ai_says_announcement in tests/test_phase32_safety.py. Evidence: evidence/phase32-safety/REPORT.md. The test reproduces the misleading model label and passes; the phrase heuristic is narrow.

Other recorded checks

Adversarial input / failureBoundary and observed outcome
House Rules injection asks the model to approve for everyoneProposal stays open; approvals remain pending; no active rule is created.
Malformed Board or Listening responseUnavailable / recoverable state; no approval rows or inferred consent.
Mediation injection demands a guilt verdictMocked path retains attributed claims and uncertainty; no guilt finding.
Private statement / threat / provider timeoutRaw text was not returned in the tested other-profile and notice route; safety pause runs before AI; timeout is sanitized.

Implemented controls

6 requests/minute in-process limit; 25-second timeout; input/output bounds; structured JSON validation; one controlled output-limit retry for House Rules / Board; sanitized metadata-only logs; SQLite membership, version, and approval checks.

Evidence limits

Most adversarial tests mock model responses. Three synthetic live probes returned HTTP 200; they cannot prove general prompt-injection resistance or fairness.

Phase 3.2 live usage: 1,564 input, 1,406 output (794 reasoning tokens within output), 13.544 s API latency. evidence/phase32-safety/live-ai-usage.json and REPORT.md. No raw prompt or roommate statement is published.

Privacy is limited: profile switching is not authentication, case participants may infer a speaker from shared details, and the keyword safety pause is not emergency support. Not a production-secure mediator.

Controls constrain state changes; they do not guarantee safe or fair model language.13 / 15

7 · Impact

Three testers saw promise—and friction.

Exploratory usability pilot, n=3. Participants tried fictional, everyday roommate-disagreement scenarios and rated their own experience. These results are descriptive perceptions, not measured household outcomes.

Overall mean · 96 points / 21 responses———4.57

What participants valued

Feedback appreciated hearing both sides and receiving a practical suggestion. Mean ratings were 5.00 for fairness and understanding, and 4.67 for practicality and preparedness.

What needs work

One participant found mediation too long and wanted a faster flow. Another asked for more personalized recommendations and clearer next steps. Clarity averaged 4.00; reuse, 3.67.

Workflow comparison, not a head-to-head test

Common approachPotential gap · product hypothesisImplemented in homi.
Roommate group chatContext and decisions can mix with unrelated messages.Separate views, clarification, approved-rule retrieval, and a persistent agreement.
Unstructured face-to-faceWho speaks first may shape what is heard; no built-in record.Each affected roommate submits a view; a shared proposal follows.
Informal verbal agreementTerms and later recollections may differ.Versioned proposal, separate approval, and stored outcome.
One-person general chatbotAdvice begins with one person’s account and may lack home rules.Both perspectives, clarifications, retrieved rules, and consent before activation.

Demonstrated

Three people completed the survey; the app ran a structured AI mediation and recorded two approvals before activating its fictional agreement. This is workflow feasibility plus positive small-sample perception.

Not demonstrated

No controlled comparison, real-household outcome, conflict reduction, time saving, or sustained adoption. No superiority over group chat or ChatGPT is established.

Next test: a larger, consented, counterbalanced comparison using the same fictional dispute in homi. and a usual-method baseline; measure completion time, fairness, next-step clarity, effort, and reuse. Survey sheets remain private; ratings were visually verified, and comments are paraphrased anonymously. Phase 3.3’s earlier “pilot pending” snapshot predates these completed surveys.

Feature comparison and n=3 perceptions are not causal evidence of real-world impact.14 / 15
8 · limits + next stepsResponsible path forward

8 · Limits + Next Steps

Trust must be built
before scale.

homi. shows how AI can structure a household conversation while leaving approval with roommates. The evidence is a prototype’s measured behavior, not a production service or impact evaluation.

Current limits

  • No real sign-in: demo profile switching cannot prove who submitted statements or cast votes. Do not use it for sensitive disclosures.
  • Private is not anonymous: a case’s participants can see a shared summary; details may reveal who said what even when names are masked.
  • Safety screen is basic: keyword-based pause is not emergency support and may miss or over-trigger concerns.
  • AI remains fallible: it can omit context, invent a weak interpretation, or produce uneven advice. Human rejection is necessary but does not guarantee fairness.
  • Service constraints: model/API dependency adds latency and failure risk; university billing was not verified and the app is not publicly hosted.
  • Financial boundary: balances and payment status are records only; no transfer or settlement verification occurs.

Next month

P1 · TRUST
Authentication and access control. Bind participant IDs to accounts, review data retention, and add a privacy design for private statements and shared summaries.
P2 · VALIDATE
Comparative pilot. Recruit a larger, consented sample; counterbalance homi. with a usual method and measure completion time, fairness, next-step clarity, effort, and reuse.
P3 · RELIABILITY
Deployment and monitoring. Add production hosting, request telemetry without sensitive text, operational alerts, and a documented recovery path.
P4 · PRODUCT
Usability response. Shorten mediation, personalize suggestions, and make next steps clearer in response to n=3 feedback; re-test before claiming benefit.
Conclusion. A roommate companion is useful only if people trust both the process and its boundaries. homi.’s strongest demonstrated idea is not an AI verdict; it is a transparent workflow in which an AI proposal stays pending until the household decides. The next proof is whether real roommates find that workflow fair, comfortable, and worth using.
